subject: FRANCOIS et al. (1960)
object: FRANCOIS et al. (1960) studied carriers of the gene for Fuchs gyrate atrophy of the choroid and retina (atrophia gyrata chorioideae et retinae). The title links the condition to Alder's anomaly.

subject: François et al. (1966)
object: François et al. (1966) wrote about gene carriers of Fuchs gyrate atrophy of the choroid and retina (atrophia gyrata choroideae et retinae).

subject: Simell and Takki (1973)
object: Simell and Takki (1973) reported that raised plasma ornithine occurs with gyrate atrophy of the choroid and retina.

subject: Takki and Simell (1974)
object: Takki and Simell (1974) discussed the genetic aspects of gyrate atrophy of the choroid and retina with hyperornithinemia.

subject: Valle et al. (1977)
object: Valle et al. (1977) measured ornithine aminotransferase (OAT; EC 2.6.1.13) activity in phytohemagglutinin-stimulated lymphocytes from a woman with gyrate atrophy of the choroid and retina and from her daughter. The patient's cells had no detectable OAT activity. The heterozygous daughter's cells had 44% of normal activity. Thymidine incorporation and other enzymes affected by transformation showed that the patient's cells were transformed. The authors concluded that these results demonstrated an enzyme deficiency in gyrate atrophy.

subject: Valle et al. (1977)
object: Valle et al. (1977) described gyrate atrophy of the choroid and retina as an inherited form of chorioretinal degeneration associated with hyperornithinemia.

subject: Kennaway et al. (1977)
object: Kennaway et al. (1977) showed that ornithine ketoacid aminotransferase activity was deficient in cultured skin fibroblasts from patients with gyrate atrophy of the choroid and retina.

subject: O'Donnell et al. (1978)
object: O'Donnell et al. (1978) found that cultured fibroblasts from a female patient with gyrate atrophy of the retina did not convert uniformly 14C-labeled L-ornithine to proline. They showed that this metabolic block was caused by deficient L-ornithine:2-oxoacid aminotransferase activity.

subject: O'Donnell et al. (1978)
object: O'Donnell et al. (1978) found that the father of the affected patient, an obligate heterozygote, had an intermediate level of L-ornithine:2-oxoacid aminotransferase activity.

subject: Shih et al. (1978)
object: Shih et al. (1978) found a virtual absence of ornithine ketoacid transaminase (OKT) activity in cultured skin fibroblasts from 5 patients with gyrate atrophy of the choroid and retina, a hyperornithinemic chorioretinal degeneration. They concluded that OKT deficiency is closely associated with the genetic defect in gyrate atrophy.

subject: Shih et al. (1978)
object: Shih et al. (1978) found that fibroblasts from 4 carrier parents of patients with gyrate atrophy showed a 42 to 65% reduction in OKT activity, consistent with the autosomal recessive inheritance of the disorder.

subject: Shih et al. (1978)
object: Shih et al. (1978) found that increasing the concentration of pyridoxal phosphate (vitamin B6) in the assay medium partially restored OKT activity in fibroblasts from 1 of 5 patients with gyrate atrophy, and concluded that genetic heterogeneity exists in this disease.

subject: Stoppoloni et al. (1978)
object: Stoppoloni et al. (1978) reported a girl aged 3 years and 9 months with hyperornithinemia and gyrate atrophy of the choroid and retina. She also had mild mental retardation, delayed language development, and speech defects.

subject: Stoppoloni et al. (1978)
object: Stoppoloni et al. (1978) found that restricting protein intake to a minimum of 0.8 g/kg/day significantly lowered plasma ornithine levels in their patient with gyrate atrophy.

subject: Sipilä et al. (1979)
object: Sipilä et al. (1979) studied 21 patients with gyrate atrophy of the choroid and retina and hyperornithinemia. The patients were not weak, but type 2 muscle fibers were atrophic and had tubular aggregates in almost all of them. Both sexes were affected equally, and this was the first disease in which tubular aggregates were shown in females. The number of type 2 fibers decreased with age.

subject: Sipilä et al. (1979)
object: Sipilä et al. (1979) suggested that the muscle and eye changes in gyrate atrophy are probably related to abnormal creatine synthesis caused by the increased body pool of ornithine. They also suggested that muscle abnormalities may be present in other tapetoretinal dystrophies.

subject: Valle et al. (1980)
object: Valle et al. (1980) studied 4 patients with gyrate atrophy of the choroid and retina, all of whom had hyperornithinemia. They also found elevated plasma histidine and decreased plasma lysine and branched-chain amino acids. Renal clearances of these amino acids were not raised enough to explain the low plasma levels.

subject: Valle et al. (1980)
object: Valle et al. (1980) put 1 patient with gyrate atrophy on an arginine-deficient diet. Plasma ornithine fell steadily from 13 times normal to the upper limit of normal, and ornithinuria and lysinuria disappeared. Oral alpha-aminoisobutyric acid sped up the fall by increasing renal ornithine losses. As ornithine neared normal, plasma lysine normalized and plasma arginine became subnormal. Over 1.5 years on a 10-20 g protein diet plus essential amino acids, plasma ornithine stayed between 55 and 355 microM. The chorioretinal degeneration did not progress, and vision apparently improved.

subject: Kennaway et al. (1980)
object: Kennaway et al. (1980) described 4 patients with hyperornithinemia and gyrate atrophy of the choroid and retina. Histochemical staining of punch muscle biopsies showed intracellular inclusions in type 2 muscle fibers, and electron microscopy showed tubular aggregates about 60 nm in diameter next to the sarcoplasmic membrane.

subject: Kennaway et al. (1980)
object: Kennaway et al. (1980) found deficient ornithine ketoacid aminotransferase (OKT) activity in cultured skin fibroblasts from all 4 patients. Obligate heterozygotes had about half-normal OKT activity. In 1 patient, an oral glucose tolerance test caused marked changes in serum ornithine and lysine levels, along with mild glucose intolerance.

subject: Kennaway et al. (1980)
object: Kennaway et al. (1980) documented an in vivo response to vitamin B6 in 3 of 4 patients: oral B6 supplementation significantly lowered fasting serum ornithine and raised lysine. In vitro, the patients' fibroblasts showed increased OKT activity at higher pyridoxal phosphate concentrations.

subject: Kennaway et al. (1980)
object: Kennaway et al. (1980) found that obligate heterozygotes had a mean serum ornithine slightly above normal, but their values overlapped considerably with the normal range. Oral ornithine tolerance tests distinguished carriers from controls in only 1 of 5 cases, whereas fibroblast OKT activity in carriers was about half normal.

subject: Sipilä et al. (1980)
object: Sipilä et al. (1980) gave intravenous arginine to 6 patients with gyrate atrophy of the choroid and retina and 6 controls. Serum arginine curves were similar in the two groups, but the rise in serum ornithine was more than 3 times greater in patients. The mean plasma ornithine half-time was 360 min in patients versus 97 min in controls, and patients cleared ornithine from the extracellular fluid significantly more slowly.

subject: Sipilä et al. (1980)
object: Sipilä et al. (1980) found that after an arginine load, urinary guanidinoacetate excretion rose sharply in all controls, more so in females. Patients with gyrate atrophy always excreted less guanidinoacetate than controls, with highly significant differences within each sex. Differences in creatine excretion were less marked.

subject: Sipilä et al. (1980)
object: Sipilä et al. (1980) concluded that in patients with gyrate atrophy, high ornithine concentrations inhibit the formation of guanidinoacetate, creatine, and possibly phosphocreatine at the transamidination step (arginine-glycine transamidinase). They suggested that a deficiency of high-energy phosphates may underlie the eye and muscle atrophies.

subject: Kaiser-Kupfer et al. (1980)
object: Kaiser-Kupfer et al. (1980) reported a female patient with gyrate atrophy of the choroid and retina who was treated with an arginine-deficient diet. Over 20 months, the diet lowered her plasma ornithine concentration fivefold. About 15 months after starting the diet, she noticed her vision had improved. The electroretinogram, dark adaptation and color vision also improved, mostly in rod function and to a lesser extent in cone function. The authors called the results preliminary but suggested that lowering plasma ornithine with a low-arginine diet is beneficial in this disease.

subject: McInnes et al. (1981)
object: McInnes et al. (1981) treated a 15-year-old patient with hyperornithinemia (plasma ornithine 0.6-1.2 mmol/l) and gyrate atrophy of the retina with a low-arginine diet. The diet lowered plasma ornithine to 0.15-0.25 mmol/l, close to the normal range. After 5 weeks of treatment, visual function improved in one eye that had been severely impaired, with no improvement, for 3 years. The improvement lasted until the patient stopped following the diet closely at 8 months, after which visual function regressed toward its pretreatment state.

subject: McInnes et al. (1981)
object: McInnes et al. (1981) found that restricting dietary arginine too much caused hyperammonemia in their patient. They concluded that arginine is an essential amino acid in ornithine transaminase deficiency. They suggested that lowering plasma ornithine may reverse a metabolic neuroretinopathy in this disease and might also stop the retinal atrophy from progressing.

subject: Sipilä et al. (1981)
object: Sipilä et al. (1981) gave 7 patients with gyrate atrophy 1.5 g of creatine daily as a dietary supplement. After 1 year of treatment, the diameter of type II muscle fibers increased from 34.1 +/- 7.1 to 49.9 +/- 7.0 microns (P less than 0.001), with no significant increase in type I fiber diameter. Visual-field tests showed no further constriction during therapy, and fundus photography showed slow impairment at an age otherwise associated with rapid progression. The authors described these results as promising but preliminary.

subject: Sipilä et al. (1981)
object: Sipilä et al. (1981) proposed that part of the disease mechanism in gyrate atrophy may be deficient creatine formation caused by hyperornithinemia. They suggested this leads to a shortage of cellular phosphocreatine energy stores.

subject: Sipilä et al. (1981)
object: Sipilä et al. (1981) described gyrate atrophy as characterized by progressive constriction of the visual fields, a 10- to 20-fold elevation of plasma ornithine, and reduced ornithine aminotransferase activity. They noted that atrophy of type II muscle fibers is morphologically conspicuous but clinically unimportant, and that it progresses together with the eye disease.

subject: Sipilä et al. (1981)
object: Sipilä et al. (1981) found trace ornithine aminotransferase activity in liver tissue from 2 patients with gyrate atrophy of the choroid and retina with hyperornithinemia. The mutant enzyme's Km for ornithine was 200 mM, 50-fold higher than normal. Raising alpha-oxoglutarate and pyridoxal 5-prime-phosphate to 10 times the concentrations that gave maximal activity of the normal enzyme had no effect on the mutant enzyme. Ornithine concentrations above 70 mM inhibited the normal enzyme, but the mutant enzyme showed no substrate inhibition even at 1,000 mM ornithine.

subject: Sipilä et al. (1981)
object: Based on the kinetic data, Sipilä et al. (1981) suggested that the abnormal ornithine aminotransferase in the 2 patients they studied has an altered binding site for ornithine.

subject: Sipilä et al. (1981)
object: Sipilä et al. (1981) described gyrate atrophy of the choroid and retina with hyperornithinemia as an autosomal recessive disease that leads to blindness and is associated with deficient ornithine aminotransferase activity.

subject: Fukuda et al. (1983)
object: Fukuda et al. (1983) measured free amino acid concentrations in erythrocytes, lymphocytes, and granulocytes from 2 brothers with gyrate atrophy of the choroid and retina and hyperornithinemia. Ornithine concentrations were raised in the blood cells, with the degree of elevation depending on cell type, and aspartic acid concentrations were low in erythrocytes.

subject: Fukuda et al. (1983)
object: Fukuda et al. (1983) followed free amino acid concentrations in blood cells of the 2 brothers for up to 24 hours after an oral dose of ornithine. Ornithine in blood cells peaked 2 hours after the dose and stayed high for at least 4 hours, but after 2 hours the concentration curves differed among erythrocytes, lymphocytes, and granulocytes.

subject: Kaiser-Kupfer et al. (1983)
object: Kaiser-Kupfer et al. (1983) described the cataract in 9 phakic patients with gyrate atrophy of the choroid and retina. The lens opacities were located mainly along the confluence of the posterior sutures and interfered with vision because they lay in the visual axis. The authors concluded that by the second decade, cataract is a uniform finding in gyrate atrophy and appears to be unique compared with cataracts associated with other forms of retinal degeneration.

subject: Kaiser-Kupfer et al. (1983)
object: Kaiser-Kupfer et al. (1983) examined 3 cataractous lenses removed from patients with gyrate atrophy aged 31 to 47 years, both by gross inspection and under the microscope. On histology, the posterior suture region was filled with liquefied, degenerated lens material that resembled typical senile cataract changes.

subject: Wirtz et al. (1985)
object: Wirtz et al. (1985) studied fibroblasts from 4 pyridoxine-responsive and 3 non-responsive patients with gyrate atrophy of the choroid and retina. Cells from responsive patients had higher ornithine ketoacid transaminase (OKT) activity in homogenates and more incorporation of radioactivity from 14C-ornithine into protein in cultured cells in situ than cells from non-responsive patients.

subject: Wirtz et al. (1985)
object: Wirtz et al. (1985) performed complementation analysis on fused fibroblasts from the 7 patients, measuring the ratio of 14C/3H incorporation into protein after incubation in 14C-ornithine and 3H-leucine. Crosses showed no positive complementation, and the authors suggested that pyridoxine-responsive and non-responsive gyrate atrophy are caused by different allelic mutations at the same OKT locus.

subject: Barrett et al. (1987)
object: Barrett et al. (1987) used a cDNA clone encoding human ornithine aminotransferase (OAT) to map OAT gene sequences by somatic cell hybrids and in situ hybridization to chromosome regions 10q26 and Xp11.2.

subject: Barrett et al. (1987)
object: Barrett et al. (1987) reviewed 80 biochemically confirmed cases of gyrate atrophy and found that the data confirmed autosomal recessive inheritance and supported the presence of a functional OAT gene on chromosome 10.

subject: Barrett et al. (1987)
object: Barrett et al. (1987) noted that the X-chromosome OAT gene sequences at Xp11.2 mapped to the same region as L1.28 (Xp11.0-p11.3), a marker closely linked to X-linked recessive retinitis pigmentosa.

subject: Ramesh et al. (1988)
object: Ramesh et al. (1988) defined 6 RFLPs at the ornithine aminotransferase (OAT) locus, all mapping to chromosome 10, with an overall heterozygosity of 83%. Using these RFLPs, they found that the OAT locus segregated concordantly with gyrate atrophy in 1 available pedigree. The RFLPs also showed significant linkage disequilibrium with GA, which the authors took as genetic evidence that a defect in the OAT structural gene causes the disorder.

subject: Ramesh et al. (1988)
object: Ramesh et al. (1988) suggested that the OAT RFLPs could be used for prenatal diagnosis and carrier detection in families with a previous history of gyrate atrophy. They added that the RFLPs would also allow identification of haplotypes associated with GA chromosomes.

subject: Shih et al. (1988)
object: Shih et al. (1988) found that cultured fibroblasts from heterozygotes for both the pyridoxine-responsive and the pyridoxine-nonresponsive variants of gyrate atrophy contained intermediate levels of ornithine ketoacid transaminase (OKT) activity.

subject: Shih et al. (1988)
object: Shih et al. (1988) showed that carriers of the pyridoxine-responsive and pyridoxine-nonresponsive forms of gyrate atrophy could be distinguished by the in vitro response of fibroblast OKT activity to pyridoxal phosphate (PLP). The ratio of OKT activity at 0.04 mM PLP to that at 0 mM PLP was lowest in controls (1.18 +/- 0.18; n = 12), intermediate in pyridoxine-nonresponsive heterozygotes (1.43 +/- 0.26; n = 5), and highest in pyridoxine-responsive heterozygotes (2.20 +/- 0.14; n = 3).

subject: Mitchell et al. (1988)
object: Mitchell et al. (1988) studied 4 Lebanese patients with gyrate atrophy from 2 pedigrees. RNase A protection with antisense RNA probes showed a probe-target mismatch at the 5-prime end of the first coding exon of OAT. PCR amplification and sequencing of genomic DNA showed a G-to-A transition that changed the initiator ATG (methionine) codon to ATA, and the mutation segregated with the GA allele in both pedigrees. Initiation of translation at the closest in-frame methionine codon would truncate OAT by 138 amino acids, removing the entire mitochondrial leader sequence and 113 amino acids of the mature peptide.

subject: OAT G----A transition, changing the initiator ATG (methionine) codon to ATA
object: OAT

subject: Mitchell et al. (1988)
object: Mitchell et al. (1988) described gyrate atrophy of the choroid and retina as an autosomal recessive chorioretinal degeneration caused by deficiency of the mitochondrial matrix enzyme ornithine-delta-aminotransferase (OAT).

subject: Kennaway et al. (1989)
object: Kennaway et al. (1989) characterized mutant ornithine aminotransferase (OAT) in fibroblast mitochondria from 9 patients with gyrate atrophy of the choroid and retina, 4 of whom were pyridoxine-responsive, using a sensitive radiochemical assay. The apparent Km for pyridoxal phosphate (PLP) was higher in pyridoxine-responsive patients than in nonresponsive patients, whose apparent Km for PLP was normal; the apparent Km for ornithine was normal in the 7 patients studied. These data clarified the mechanism of pyridoxine response.

subject: Kennaway et al. (1989)
object: Kennaway et al. (1989) found that, surprisingly, the pyridoxine-responsive patient with the mildest clinical disease had the highest Km for PLP; however, she had the most stable OAT enzyme on heat-stability testing at 45 degrees C, which the authors presumed contributed to her milder phenotype.

subject: Kennaway et al. (1989)
object: Kennaway et al. (1989) found by Western blot analysis of mitochondrial proteins with antibody to human OAT clearly detectable OAT protein in pyridoxine-responsive patients and in 2 of 5 nonresponders, but low or undetectable levels in the other 3 patients, indicating heterogeneity within as well as between the pyridoxine-responsive and nonresponsive patients with gyrate atrophy.

subject: Brody et al. (1992)
object: Brody et al. (1992) surveyed the ornithine delta-aminotransferase (OAT) genes of patients with gyrate atrophy of the choroid and retina and discovered and molecularly characterized 21 newly recognized OAT alleles, demonstrating extensive allelic heterogeneity.

subject: Brody et al. (1992)
object: Brody et al. (1992) determined the consequences of 21 new and 3 previously described OAT mutations on OAT mRNA, antigen, and enzyme activity in cultured fibroblasts from gyrate atrophy patients: 20 of 24 alleles produced normal amounts of normally sized OAT mRNA, whereas only 2 of 24 had normal amounts of OAT antigen.

subject: Brody et al. (1992)
object: Brody et al. (1992) reproduced OAT mutations by site-directed mutagenesis and expressed the mutant enzymes in Chinese hamster ovary cells, confirming that several of the mutations inactivate OAT and cause gyrate atrophy in these patients.

subject: Brody et al. (1992)
object: Brody et al. (1992) noted that inherited deficiency of ornithine delta-aminotransferase, a nuclear-encoded mitochondrial matrix enzyme, results in ornithine accumulation and a characteristic chorioretinal degeneration, gyrate atrophy of the choroid and retina.

subject: Wang et al. (1995)
object: Wang et al. (1995) used gene targeting to produce OAT-deficient mice. As neonates, the mice had hypoornithinemia and died, but short-term arginine supplementation rescued them. After weaning they developed hyperornithinemia like that of human GA patients. Over several months they developed a retinal degeneration involving the photoreceptors and pigment epithelium, and the authors concluded that OAT-deficient mice appear to be an excellent model of human GA.

subject: Wang et al. (1995)
object: Following the mouse findings, Wang et al. (1995) studied one human infant with GA and found transient hypoornithinemia. They concluded that the OAT reaction plays opposite roles in neonatal and adult mammals.

subject: Valtonen et al. (1996)
object: Valtonen et al. (1996) examined the thigh muscles of 7 patients with gyrate atrophy using semi-open conchotome muscle biopsies, CT, and ultralow-field (0.02 T) MRI. Type 2 muscle fiber atrophy was found in all biopsy samples and tubular aggregates in 6 of 7 samples.

subject: Valtonen et al. (1996)
object: Valtonen et al. (1996) found that CT density of thigh muscle was increased in the only child studied, decreased in 3 elderly patients, and normal in the remaining 3. Mean MRI T1 relaxation times were decreased in patients compared with 6 healthy controls (135 vs 157 ms, p = 0.002), whereas T2 was slightly but not significantly increased; the authors concluded that thigh muscles of GA patients universally show changes on CT and MRI, but relaxation time measurements gave little additional information on muscle metabolism.

subject: Valtonen et al. (1999)
object: Valtonen et al. (1999) studied central nervous system involvement in 23 untreated patients with gyrate atrophy (mean age 32 +/- 18 years) and compared them with age-matched healthy controls. Brain MRI showed degenerative white matter lesions in 50% of patients, and 70% had premature atrophic changes, with a striking increase in the number of Virchow (perivascular) spaces. Of the patients who had an EEG, 58% had abnormal slow background activity, focal lesions, or high-amplitude beta rhythm (more than 50 microV). The EEG findings were not associated with the MRI changes or with the patients' age or sex. The authors concluded that early degenerative and atrophic brain changes and an abnormal EEG are features of gyrate atrophy, in addition to the known eye and muscle manifestations.

subject: Valtonen et al. (1999)
object: Valtonen et al. (1999) found that the brain MRI and EEG findings in 9 patients with gyrate atrophy who had taken creatine or creatine precursor supplements daily for several years did not differ from those of 23 untreated patients.

subject: Valtonen et al. (1999)
object: Valtonen et al. (1999) noted that the retinal and choroidal degeneration and the type II muscle fiber atrophy with tubular aggregates in gyrate atrophy have been suggested to be caused by a deficiency of phosphocreatine induced by hyperornithinemia. Because guanidinoacetate methyltransferase deficiency, another disorder of creatine metabolism, causes abnormal brain MRI and EEG findings, they studied the central nervous system in gyrate atrophy, which appears to involve a milder degree of phosphocreatine deficiency.

subject: Wang et al. (2000)
object: Wang et al. (2000) maintained Oat-null (Oat -/-) mice, produced by gene targeting, on an arginine-restricted diet for 12 months and monitored them by plasma amino acid measurement, electroretinography, and retinal histologic and ultrastructural studies. The diet substantially reduced plasma ornithine levels and completely prevented retinal degeneration in the Oat -/- mice.

subject: Wang et al. (2000)
object: Wang et al. (2000) concluded from the prevention of retinal degeneration by an arginine-restricted diet in Oat -/- mice that ornithine accumulation is a necessary factor in the pathophysiology of the retinal degeneration in gyrate atrophy, and that restoring OAT activity in the retina is not required for effective treatment.

subject: Caruso et al. (2001)
object: Caruso et al. (2001) assessed the course of change in visual function in 5 patients with gyrate atrophy before a gene replacement therapy clinical trial, using visual field sensitivity and electroretinogram amplitude as outcome variables and calculating their half-lives. Over 4 to 6 years of follow-up, median visual field half-lives were 17.0 years by static perimetry and 11.4 years by kinetic perimetry, and median electroretinogram half-lives were 16.0 years for the maximal response and 10.7 years for the flicker response. The authors concluded that visual function frequently declines slowly.

subject: Caruso et al. (2001)
object: Caruso et al. (2001) concluded that, because visual function in gyrate atrophy often declines slowly, a long-term clinical trial would be needed to assess whether gene replacement therapy preserves visual function.

subject: Kaiser-Kupfer et al. (2002)
object: Kaiser-Kupfer et al. (2002) reported 2 pairs of sibs with gyrate atrophy who had been on an arginine-restricted diet to lower plasma ornithine for 16 to 17 years. In each pair, the younger sib started the diet at an earlier age than the older sib, and the younger sib's chorioretinal lesions progressed more slowly. The authors concluded that long-term, substantial reduction of plasma ornithine, if begun early, may appreciably slow the progression of chorioretinal lesions and, to a lesser extent, the progressive loss of retinal function.

subject: Peltola et al. (2002)
object: Peltola et al. (2002) looked for peripheral nervous system involvement in 40 patients with gyrate atrophy (mean age 31.6 +/- 16.3 years; range 5 to 74 years) using neurography, quantitative sensory threshold testing, and evoked potential testing. Neurography was abnormal in 21 patients (53%), and the abnormalities were associated with patient age and with the severity of the ophthalmologic changes. Quantitative sensory threshold testing showed abnormal large-fiber function in 7 patients (18%) and abnormal small-fiber function in 4 patients (10%). Somatosensory and brainstem auditory evoked potential responses were abolished in 5 patients.

subject: Peltola et al. (2002)
object: Peltola et al. (2002) described gyrate atrophy as an inborn error of amino acid metabolism caused by mutations in ornithine aminotransferase. Its features are hyperornithinemia, progressive centripetal loss of vision, minor CNS abnormalities, and type II muscle fiber atrophy with accumulation of tubular aggregates. From the peripheral nerve findings, they concluded that gyrate atrophy is a systemic disease that affects the peripheral nervous system as well as the CNS.

subject: Balfoort et al. (2021)
object: Balfoort et al. (2021) carried out a systematic review following PRISMA guidelines of therapeutic interventions in GACR. They identified 33 studies covering 107 patients, mostly case reports (27) or case series (4), and found no randomized controlled trials or large cohort studies. Protein-restricted diets lowered ornithine levels by 16.0 to 91.2%. Pyridoxine responsiveness was reported in 30% of the included mutations. Lysine supplementation decreased ornithine levels by 21 to 34%. Other treatments reported were creatine or creatine precursor supplementation and proline supplementation.

subject: Balfoort et al. (2021)
object: Balfoort et al. (2021) concluded that a protein-restricted diet, pyridoxine supplementation (depending on the variant), and/or lysine supplementation can reduce ornithine levels. Because the included studies lacked predefined clinical outcome measures and structured follow-up, the authors could not draw conclusions about clinical effectiveness. They noted that there is no curative treatment and no international treatment protocol.

subject: Balfoort et al. (2021)
object: Balfoort et al. (2021) described GACR as a rare inborn error of amino acid metabolism caused by biallelic variants in the OAT gene. It is characterized by vision decline in early life that eventually leads to complete blindness, and by high plasma ornithine levels.
